node-1.label: Left scrotal soreness and oedema for five days

node-2.label: Patient is a 13-year-old boy with no lower urinary tract symptoms and no major relevant medical or surgical history

node-3.label: Based on penile characteristics, the patient was diagnosed with occult penis; other congenital anomalies of the genitourinary tract were excluded based on imaging findings

node-4.label: Physical examination revealed an enlarged testis, epididymis, and infected appendages; no torsion was evident in the sperm vessels, but purulent foci were visible on the surface of the vessels with a tough and inseparable texture; the patient was at Tanner stage G4P4

why.why: The Laboratory_Physician and Radiologist analyses confirm leukocytosis and P. aeruginosa growth, and Doppler ultrasound shows an enlarged left testis with heterogeneous echo, enhanced vascularity, and preserved blood flow; these support acute epididymo-orchitis. Negative urinalysis and occult penis favor primary scrotal infection. Although surgical exploration has not been performed, the convergent infectious findings raise confidence from 0.78 to 0.92.

Radiologist analysis notes preserved/retained blood flow in the enlarged left testis, ruling out torsion; P. aeruginosa growth and purulent foci indicate infection rather than torsion. A mild whirlpool sign on follow-up is a minor concern but is outweighed by preserved blood flow and infectious findings, reducing confidence from 0.12 to 0.05.

Doppler shows a hypervascular inflammatory pattern rather than a typical tumor mass, and culture confirms P. aeruginosa pyogenic infection; the Laboratory_Physician and Radiologist analyses both consider tumor unlikely. These infectious findings reduce confidence from 0.10 to 0.05.
